opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly one we don't have a perfect answer to yet. In language and vision you can point to the scale of internet data and say, okay, we've covered a lot of the distribution. In robotics there's no internet of robot actions, so we have to think much more carefully about what kind of diversity matters.

The way I tend to think about it is along a few axes. One is environmental diversity: how many different homes, kitchens, offices, lighting conditions, and backgrounds has the robot seen? We've found that this matters a lot. If you collect a huge amount of data in one or two lab environments, the robot can get very good there, but it falls apart in a new kitchen. Spreading that same amount of data across many more locations tends to generalize much better.

Another axis is object diversity: different shapes, materials, and deformable versus rigid objects. Then there's task and behavior diversity: not just picking and placing, but wiping, folding, opening, and all the little recovery behaviors when something goes wrong. That last part is underrated. If all of your data is clean, successful demonstrations, the robot never learns what to do when it slightly misgrasps something, and in the real world that happens constantly.

There's also embodiment diversity, meaning data from different robot arms and platforms. We've seen some encouraging signs that training across embodiments helps rather than hurts, because the model learns something more general about physical interaction.

As for how we actually assess it, the most honest answer is empirically. We hold out environments and objects the robot has never seen, deploy it there, and measure how it does. Proxy metrics like counting scenes or objects are useful, but they don't fully capture whether you've covered the things that matter. So a lot of it is building evaluations that look like the real deployment conditions, being disciplined about truly held-out settings, and then using where the robot fails to tell you what kind of data to go collect next. It's a feedback loop more than a formula.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because breadth is really the thing that matters. If you just look at the number of hours of data a robot has, that's actually not a very good proxy for whether it's going to generalize. You can collect a thousand hours of a robot doing one task in one lab, and it'll be great at that task in that lab and fall apart the moment you move it to a different kitchen.

So the way I tend to think about it is along a few axes. One is diversity of scenes and objects. How many different environments has the robot seen? How many different instances of a category, like different mugs, different drawers, different lighting conditions? Another is diversity of tasks and behaviors, so not just pick and place, but folding, pouring, opening things, manipulating deformable objects. And then there's diversity of embodiments, which has become really important recently, because a lot of the large-scale datasets, like Open X-Embodiment, are pulling together data from many different robots with different arms, different grippers, different camera placements.

The way we actually assess it, though, is almost always empirically. You hold out things. You hold out an object the robot has never seen, a scene it's never been in, a task it's never done, and you measure how performance degrades as you move further from the training distribution. And what you find is that the slope of that curve tells you a lot more than the absolute performance on in-distribution tasks. A robot that gets 90 percent in the lab and 10 percent in a new home has not really learned something general. A robot that's at 70 and 60 is in a much better place, even though the headline number is worse.

The other thing I'd say is that it's hard to do this with benchmarks alone, because the real world is just so much more varied than any benchmark we can construct. So a lot of what we do is take the robot somewhere it's never been, like an actual house or an actual office, and see what happens. That's expensive and slow, but I don't think there's a substitute for it right now. And honestly, one of the lessons from language models is that the breadth of the pretraining data mattered more than almost anyone expected, and I think we're seeing the same thing start to play out in robotics.

r001.rationale: The response proposes assessing generalization through held-out objects, scenes, and tasks and measuring performance degradation. It does not say there is no clear way to measure how different tasks are from one another.

r002.rationale: It identifies diversity of scenes and objects as an axis of breadth and asks how many different environments the robot has seen, communicating environment count as an indicator of experience breadth.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is what kind of diversity the robot is getting, rather than just how many hours of experience it has. If you have a robot do the same task in the same environment over and over again, it might get very good at that task, but that doesn’t necessarily tell you whether it can handle a new environment.

So I’d look at variation across objects, across tasks, across environments, and even across things like camera viewpoints. And then you have to evaluate on things you deliberately held out. Can it pick up an object it hasn’t seen before? Can it do a familiar task in a new kitchen? Can it combine skills in a way that wasn’t demonstrated during training?

Those are different kinds of generalization. A system might be quite good at one and struggle with another. So I don’t think there’s a single number that captures the breadth of experience. What matters is whether that experience gives it the coverage it needs for the situations you want it to handle.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is whether the robot has seen variation along the dimensions that matter for the task. You can collect thousands of demonstrations in one kitchen, but if they all involve the same objects, the same lighting, and the same camera position, that may actually be a pretty narrow set of experiences.

So I’d look at what happens when you change those things. Can it manipulate an object it hasn’t seen before? Can it do the task in a different kitchen? Can it recover when the object slips or someone puts something in its way? Those are different kinds of generalization, and being good at one doesn’t necessarily imply being good at the others.

The difficult part is that we don’t yet have a great way to reduce that breadth to a single number. The number of hours of data tells you something, but you also need to understand how diverse those hours are. Ultimately, you have to evaluate on situations that are meaningfully different from the training data and see where the robot succeeds and where it breaks.
